mnemonic: A receptionist ends every sentence with a small dip of the head, and every dip carries the same soft sound: "cah", car with the R swallowed. Women hang it on the end of a statement the way the head dips. Leave it off and the sentence lands bare. (↓ falling, the head drops with the voice)
scene: A hotel receptionist in a neat uniform standing behind a marble desk, head bowed and palms pressed together toward a guest she is handing a key to. Her whole posture is a small polite dip.

mnemonic: A market vendor holds up a mango; the customer points at his own chest — "MY?" — voice climbing at the end the way an English question does. That climb is the question: ไหม turns any sentence into one. (↑ rising, the voice lifts like an eyebrow)
scene: Bustling Thai street market at golden hour. A smiling vendor in an apron holds a ripe mango out across her fruit stall. Facing her, a young foreign traveller points at his own chest with both index fingers, eyebrows raised high, mouth open in an exaggerated questioning expression.

mnemonic: A vendor lifts a glass of orange tea and raises her eyebrows: this one? The customer nods once, hard. "Châi." Yes — chai, that is the one. (↓ falling, the voice drops with the nod)
scene: A morning tea cart where the vendor holds a tall glass of milky orange iced tea up across the counter, eyebrows raised in question, while the customer opposite nods once, firmly, finger already pointing at the glass. Ice bucket, steam, sunlit street.

mnemonic: The cow lows exactly when the pail is set down, not a moment before. Say moo with the lips pulled wide in a grin instead of pushed forward and you have mɯ̂a: the word that marks the moment something happens. (↓ falling, the moo drops away at the end)
scene: A dairy shed at dawn. A farmer crouched on a low stool has just set a steel pail down under a cow, whose head is thrown back mid-bellow, mouth wide. Straw, a hanging lamp, cold blue light through the open door.

mnemonic: The place word thîi plus the knee of นี้ — this place. A man on a picnic blanket taps his own knee, then the grass right beside it: here, not over there, right at the knee. (↓ both syllables drop, each one planted)
scene: A man sitting cross-legged on a picnic blanket in a park, tapping his own knee with one hand and pressing his other flat on the grass beside the blanket. A friend standing a few metres away holds a basket, hesitating.

mnemonic: Someone asks how he does it and the man taps his own chest with the butt of his cue: because he is a pro. That is the whole answer — prɔ́, the word that hands you the reason. (▲ high and taut, snapped out with the tap of the cue)
scene: A snooker hall. A man in a waistcoat leans on his cue after a shot, tapping his own chest with two fingers, eyebrows raised, entirely unbothered. Onlookers round the table stare at the perfectly potted balls. Low hanging lamp, green baize, smoke.

mnemonic: The type word yàang plus rai, what: what way? A cook is asked how she gets the noodles to fly like that and simply holds her wrist up mid-toss. Yàang-rai is how — the manner of doing a thing. (— the second syllable levels out, the question left hanging)
scene: A street kitchen. A cook holds a wok up and away from the flame with noodles and beansprouts in mid-air above it, her wrist cocked. An apprentice stares from the side, his own wok untouched. Night market lights, fire, steam.

mnemonic: nák- is the prefix Thai sticks on the front of anyone who does a thing. Hear it as a knack — the boy with a knack for it — and glue it to riian, to study. Knack for studying: a student. Learn nák- once and it hands you a dozen other people. (— riian levels out flat and patient at the end)
scene: A Thai schoolboy in a crisp white uniform sits at a wooden classroom desk, effortlessly spinning a globe on one fingertip while his classmates twist round in their seats to watch, delighted. Morning sun through louvred shutters, dust hanging in the light.

mnemonic: Stick a hum on the front of 'earn' and you have it: ngɤɤn. At closing time the stallholder counts the day's takings into a biscuit tin, note by note. What she earned is what the word means — money, and silver before that. (— flat and level, coin after coin)
scene: A market stall after closing, shutters half down. A woman sits on a stool counting banknotes into a battered biscuit tin on her lap, coins stacked on the counter beside her. One hanging bulb, everything else dark.

mnemonic: Three friends order; two have chosen and the third is still reading. The waitress turns to her with one eyebrow up and a single syllable: khun lâ — and you? Lâ is the nudge that throws the question back at someone. (↓ falling, the voice drops as the eyebrow goes up)
scene: A restaurant table of three. A waitress with a notepad has turned to the last diner, pen poised, one eyebrow raised. Two friends watch the third, who is still hidden behind a tall folded card held up to her face.

mnemonic: Halfway across the tarmac the traveller stops, turns to the ground crew and asks which way the gate is — tǎam — the voice climbing the way every question climbs. Take the tarm off tarmac and you have the Thai for ask. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like a hand going up)
scene: An airport apron at dusk. A traveller with a wheeled case has halted mid-stride on wet tarmac and turned to a ground marshal in a hi-vis vest, palms open in a questioning gesture. The marshal points away toward distant terminal lights.

mnemonic: The one Thai particle that translates itself: jâ is ja, the German yes, and it carries the same warm agreement — an aunt answering a small child, a friend saying of course. Women use it where the conversation is friendly rather than formal. (↓ falling, warm and settled)
scene: A kitchen doorway. An aunt in an apron leans down nodding at a small child who is holding up an empty bowl with both hands. Steam from a pot behind her, worn tiles, warm afternoon light.

mnemonic: You jàai for your chai. The two words sit almost on top of each other — the drink and the paying for it — so every cup you buy is a free rehearsal. (▁ low, the flat sound of coins going down on the counter)
scene: A tea stall counter. A customer's hand places a small stack of coins down on the wooden counter beside a steaming glass of milky orange Thai iced tea. The vendor's hand is reaching for the coins from the other side. Close low-angle crop on the counter, warm steam, sunlit street behind.

mnemonic: A rap on the door, and the man opens it to a courier holding out a parcel. He takes it, both hands. Ráp is to receive — a parcel, a guest, a phone call, a job. (▲ high and taut, quick as the knock)
scene: A front door half open. A courier on the step holds out a brown parcel; the householder has both hands on it, taking the weight. Van at the kerb behind, rain on the path, grey afternoon.

mnemonic: The shopkeeper asks what size and the customer holds up a gnat between finger and thumb: that big. kha-nàat is size — from a gnat to an elephant, it is the same word. (▁ the second syllable drops low and flat, the fingers pinching shut)
scene: A shopkeeper leaning over a counter squinting at a customer's raised hand, finger and thumb pinched almost shut on something too small to see, while the shelves behind hold enormous rolled mats beside tiny jars. Warm shop light.

mnemonic: The crowd goes rah as the car turns slowly on its stand, and a buyer at the rail holds up a fat brick of banknotes. raa-khaa — a rah and a car — is what the thing costs, and it is the one thing everybody came to hear. (— both syllables flat and level, a price stated plainly)
scene: A motor show hall. A gleaming saloon revolves slowly on a turntable under white spotlights while a ring of onlookers cheer with arms raised. At the rail a buyer in a linen suit holds a thick brick of banknotes above his head.

mnemonic: The waiter refuses to take a spoken order — everything must be sung. The customer stands, hand on heart, and sings her dinner across the restaurant. You sàng what you sung. (▁ low and flat, even when sung badly)
scene: A restaurant dining room. A woman has risen from her table, one hand on her heart and the other flung out theatrically, singing her order toward a waiter who stands to attention with notepad raised, delighted. Other diners turn to watch. Warm chandelier light, white tablecloths.

mnemonic: The bride has lost hers somewhere in a reception of two hundred guests, so she calls across the room. One man stands up in the middle of the tables, hand high, thumb jabbing at his own chest: saa, ME. A long open aah, then ME. That is the husband. (↑ sǎa climbs as the hand goes up, then mii sits flat)
scene: A crowded wedding reception. A bride in white stands on a chair scanning the room, and among the seated guests one man in a dinner jacket has risen, one hand high, the other thumb pointed at his own chest, grinning.

mnemonic: Soon, says the engineer, and the count runs down to nothing. sǔun is zero, and his fingers make the empty circle at the very moment the rocket goes. Soon arrives, the count empties out, and that emptiness is the word. (↑ rising, the voice climbs as the count runs out)
scene: A dim mission control room at night. An engineer leans back from a glowing console, one hand raised making a circle with thumb and forefinger, eyes on the wide window where a rocket lifts off its pad in a bloom of white exhaust.

mnemonic: The tong from ต้อง with 'karn' after it. Wanting is a mild kind of must: the man in the flooded basement must have the tong, and the woman at the hardware counter tɔ̂ng-kaan a new pair. It is want with a spine in it. (— the second syllable levels out, the demand stated plainly)
scene: A hardware shop counter. A woman holds up a pair of tongs snapped clean in half toward the shopkeeper, who is already turning to a wall of new ones. Racked tools floor to ceiling, strip lighting.

mnemonic: The doorman looks at one face after another and says nah to each of them. Nâa is the face — and also the front of anything: the front of the queue, the front of a shirt, the week in front of this one. (↓ falling, flat refusal straight to the face)
scene: A club doorway at night. A doorman's flat palm rests against the chest of the next man in line while he looks past him at the others. Red lamp above the door, velvet rope, faces in the queue.

mnemonic: Rian is lean and learn in one word: the boy at the back is bent so far over his desk that his nose is nearly on the page. Rian is to study, and Thais themselves often say the r as an l. (— flat and level, the long hours)
scene: A classroom at dusk with every desk empty but one. A boy is bent right down over his desk, nose almost touching it, a small lamp beside him. Chalk dust, shuttered windows, blue light outside.

mnemonic: The decorator dabs a mark of paint along the wall at exactly the height of his string line, each dab level with the last one. Rá-dàp is the level: the grade, the rank, the height a thing has got to. (▁ the second syllable drops low, the dab lands)
scene: A bare room being decorated. A hand dabs paint onto a wall in a row of small marks that follow a taut string line pinned across it. Ladder, dust sheets, open tin on the floor. Flat daylight.

mnemonic: An electrician holds his meter up to a bare bulb to see how many watts it is pulling, and the needle swings across and settles. wát is that act — measuring, finding out how much of a thing there actually is. (▲ high and tight, the needle flicking up the dial)
scene: A dim workshop. An electrician on a wooden stepladder holds a handheld meter up toward a bare bulb hanging on a cable, its needle mid-swing across a round dial, his face lit warm from below by the filament.

mnemonic: The stylist keeps adding rollers to the perm — one more, one more, pʰɤ̂ɤm — until the head is twice the size it started. pʰɤ̂ɤm is to add on top of what is already there: more curls, more chilli, more money. (↓ falling and firm, another roller clamped on)
scene: A salon chair under warm bulb-framed mirrors. A woman's head is piled absurdly high with dozens of coloured curlers, and the stylist leans in with yet another one held ready in her fingers, both of them laughing at the size of it.

mnemonic: She asked for one carrot. The grocer hands over a pack so enormous she has to hug it with both arms, greens bursting out of the top and over her face, the single carrot still held up in her fingers. A whole pack of phàk. (▁ low and clipped, stopped dead by the k)
scene: A small woman staggers backwards under an enormous wrapped pack of vegetables held in both arms, leafy greens bursting over her face, one carrot pinched in her fingers. The grocer grins behind his stall. Bright morning market.

mnemonic: The sweep climbs down off the last chimney on the terrace, black with soot, and pulls his crooked tie straight. Soot and tie: sùt-tʰáai, the final one, the end of the row with nothing after it. (▲ tʰáai lifts high, the voice rising on the last of them)
scene: Dusk on a long terrace rooftop. A soot-blackened chimney sweep stands on the very last chimney pot of a row that recedes into the distance, straightening his crooked tie, brushes slung over one shoulder. Orange sun low behind the rooftops, smoke drifting.

mnemonic: Every morning at the same hour he packs a tea into the same dented flask and takes the same seat on the same bus. pà-kà-tì — pack a tea — is the way things normally are: ordinary, usual, nothing out of place. (▁ low and flat throughout, nothing remarkable happens)
scene: A small kitchen at dawn. A middle-aged man in a work shirt spoons tea into a dented steel flask; his lunch tin, coat and keys are laid out on the table in exactly their usual places.

mnemonic: A man at the bar holds one finger up over the crowd. Say noong — but grinning, lips pulled wide rather than rounded — and you land the Thai vowel: nɯ̀ng. One finger, one beer, one short low syllable. (▁ low and short, over almost before it starts)
scene: A crowded bar counter at night. A man leans in with one index finger raised high above the heads around him, grinning broadly with his lips pulled wide; the barman is already reaching for a glass.

mnemonic: Thai cannot begin a word with sp, so it slips a tiny sa in front and comes out with sa-bpeen: Spain, with a step taken in the doorway first. The heel comes down on the tiles and the guitar answers it. (— bpeen stays flat and level, like the long note held under the stamping)
scene: A sunlit whitewashed courtyard. A flamenco dancer in a red ruffled dress is caught mid-stamp, back arched, one arm curved high above her head; a guitarist sits behind her on a wooden chair, head bent over the strings.

mnemonic: A yard full of children raising a din — and a cloud of dirt with it. Every shout brings up more dust; the din and the dirt come off the same ground. din is that earth under their bare feet. (— flat and level, one steady note under the noise)
scene: A bare dusty schoolyard in hard sunlight. Half a dozen barefoot children mid-chase, mouths open shouting, a thick golden cloud of dust boiling up around their feet; their shins and hands caked with dry earth. A wall and a mango tree behind.

mnemonic: A rooster struts down the middle of the lane like he owns it — that guy. gài is chicken, and the cockerel is the guy who runs the yard: the dog steps round him, the hens get out of the way. (▁ low and flat, one short cluck)
scene: A village lane at dawn. An enormous glossy rooster struts down the centre of it, chest thrown out and tail high, while a dog and two hens step aside onto the verge. Wooden houses either side, mist between them, low golden light.

mnemonic: Allow me, says the old man, and he is away into a story that lasts an hour. The low sitting inside allow is lâw: to tell, to narrate, to spin the whole thing out while everyone leans in closer. (↓ falling, the voice drops as he settles into it)
scene: Night. A village elder sits on a low stool beside a cooking fire, hands mid-gesture shaping something large in the air, mouth open in speech. A ring of children and adults sit close around him, faces lit orange, leaning in.

mnemonic: A rat is sitting up in the great carved chair at the head of the marble chamber, and the ministers file in and bow to it anyway. Wherever the power happens to be sitting, that is the rát: the state. (▲ high and taut, the way a title is announced)
scene: A marble parliamentary chamber with columns and tiered benches. A large brown rat sits upright in the ornate carved chair on the raised dais, tail curled over the armrest. Two rows of officials in dark suits bow toward it, heads down.

mnemonic: At the end of the line the robot arm swings a box down and stacks it onto a wooden pallet, thump, and the pallet fills and another comes up empty behind it. pà-lìt is the making itself: what a factory does all day, every day. (▁ low and flat, the thump of the pallet taking the weight)
scene: A factory floor at the end of an assembly line. A yellow robot arm lowers a plain sealed box onto a wooden pallet already stacked shoulder-high with identical boxes; a forklift waits to one side with its forks raised.

mnemonic: Knock the s off NURSE and you have the end of sà-nɤ̌ɤ. The theatre nurse holds the tray out flat, the instrument laid on it handle first, waiting for the surgeon to take it. That is what sà-nɤ̌ɤ does with an idea: puts it forward. (↑ rising, the voice lifts as the tray comes up)
scene: An operating theatre under a bright overhead lamp. A masked nurse in a green gown extends a steel tray toward a surgeon with both hands, a single clamp laid on it turned handle first. Everything beyond the lamp's circle falls into shadow.
